s.t: Clarence Avant signed Bill Withers to Sussex Records on the strength of ‘Grandma's Hands’. Asked what was special about it, Avant replied: “Hell, everybody's got a grandma.”
s.src: Variety (Andrew Barker): An Appreciation of Bill Withers, Soul Music’s Workingman
s.q: "Grandma's Hands" was the song that convinced Clarence Avant, owner of then nascent Sussex Records, to sign Withers to his first contract in the early 1970s. ... Avant squinted at me ... and replied: "Hell, everybody's got a grandma."

s.t: Bill Withers recorded it in a single night at Wally Heider's Studio 3, on studio time Booker T. Jones borrowed from Stephen Stills: the same session as ‘Ain't No Sunshine’.
s.src: Mix: Classic Tracks: Bill Withers’ “Ain’t No Sunshine”

s.t: While making his first album, Bill Withers told producer Booker T. Jones that anyone who remembered him would remember ‘Grandma's Hands’. Years later, fans greeted him by singing it.
s.src: American Songwriter: Bill Withers: Still Bill After All These Years
s.q: The only thing that I thought was special when we did that album was telling Booker T about “Grandma’s Hands.” I said, “If anybody remembers me, they’re gonna remember me for this.” And now when people come up to me, they usually sing “Grandma’s Hands.”

s.t: Johnny Cash was such a fan of ‘Grandma's Hands’ that, meeting Bill Withers in Hawaii, he told him: “I'd like to meet your grandmother.”
s.src: Far Out: Listen to the stirring isolated vocals of Bill Withers on ‘Grandma’s Hands’
s.q: ‘Grandma’s Hands’ was so well-received that even Johnny Cash was a great fan of it. Later in life, the pair crossed paths in Hawaii ... Withers remembered: “Johnny Cash came to see me once in Hawaii, and I was surprised Johnny Cash knew who I was. He said, ‘I’d like to meet your grandmother.'”

s.t: William ‘Stylez’ Stewart played Teddy Riley the opening guitar riff and hum of Bill Withers's ‘Grandma's Hands’; Riley said that without it there would never have been ‘No Diggity’.
s.src: Complex: Bill Withers samples in rap
s.q: the opening moments of Withers’ “Grandma’s Hands”—an acoustic guitar riff and a hum—were repurposed masterfully into this 1996 jam. Teddy Riley is credited with production, but it was actually the idea of co-producer William “Stylez” Stewart to use the Withers sample. “If he hadn’t played that sample for me, there would never be a ‘No Diggity,’” Riley has admitted.

f.t: He came straight from the factory to his first album session with a notebook of songs, and asked producer Booker T. Jones who would sing them, expecting another vocalist.
f.src: Rolling Stone (Andy Greene, 2015): Bill Withers: The Soul Man Who Walked Away, reprinted by Jazz Aspen Snowmass
f.q: “Bill came right from the factory and showed up in his old brogans and his old clunk of a car with a notebook full of songs,” says Jones. “When he saw everyone in the studio, he asked to speak to me privately and said, ‘Booker, who is going to sing these songs?’ I said, ‘You are, Bill.’

f.t: In October 1971 two letters came on the same day: Weber Aircraft offering his old $3.50-an-hour mechanic's job back, and Johnny Carson's The Tonight Show inviting him to sing.
f.q: In October 1971, Withers received two letters on the same day. The first was from his former employer Weber Aircraft, which had laid him off a few months earlier. It offered Withers his mechanic's job, which paid $3.50 an hour. The second letter was from Johnny Carson's The Tonight Show, inviting Withers to sing "Ain't No Sunshine" on NBC.

f.t: A classic late bloomer, he was in his late twenties before he ever picked up a guitar, and well into his thirties before he had an album out.
f.src: Variety (Andrew Barker): An Appreciation of Bill Withers, Soul Music’s Workingman

f.t: On ‘Lovely Day’ he holds a high E for 18 seconds, the longest sustained note on an American chart hit.
f.q: With "Lovely Day", Withers set the record for the longest sustained note on an American chart hit, holding a high E for 18 seconds.

f.t: He called his 2015 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction “an award of attrition”, adding: “I don't think I've done bad for a guy from Slab Fork, West Virginia.”
f.src: Rolling Stone (Andy Greene, 2015): Bill Withers: The Soul Man Who Walked Away, reprinted by Jazz Aspen Snowmass
